s17.slug: SUNDAY · 9:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, UPSTAIRS — THE TUB
body: The bath is already run when he gets to the top of the stairs. The bathroom door stands open, and the only light in there is two candles — one on the sill of the open window, one on the floor by the tub’s back foot — and past them the moon over the Channel, still full, or near enough, white on the water and white across the old tile, black and white hexagons, half of them cracked since before Sol was born. The tub stands in the middle of the floor on four iron claws, deep and white and steaming. Her iPod sits on the edge of the sink in a speaker no bigger than a hymnal, turned low: a harpsichord picking its way down over a drum as slow as a pulse, and a woman’s voice somewhere far inside it, too far in to make out a word.
The only other clawfoot Jack has ever known stands on its end in the side yard on Glenwood, painted blue inside, with the Blessed Mother in it and Nonna’s geraniums at her feet.

Skye is in the doorway in a white towel, her hair twisted up off her neck with a pencil stuck through it to hold it. Before he’s off the last stair she puts her hand on his chest, the fingers spread over his sweatshirt, over his heart, and keeps it there, and looks up at him, and says it.
“I watched you go up,” she says. “I kept my word all week. I’m asking. Not this minute. Tonight. I wanted you to hear it before anything, so you’d know it isn’t the bath talking.”

body.text: “You got there first on Wednesday,” she says. “I’m getting *this* first.”
body.else: “I’m going first this time,” she says.

body: He doesn’t answer yet. Her hand stays where it is, and his heart goes on telling it whatever it’s telling it, and she lets it talk as long as it wants, and she doesn’t make him.

She has done it the one way he has no argument ready for: first, in words, before anything, in a towel at the top of Sol’s stairs, with this morning still on him. He looks at her in the candlelight with her chin up and her hand on his heart, and he loves her so much it makes him stupid.

She takes the hand back. She lets the towel go onto the bathmat like a towel, steps over the high white side into the water, and sits down in it to her shoulders. “Get in, Youngstown. That’s my second bath. The first one went cold while I practiced.”

He gets out of his clothes by the sink with his back to the mirror — the sweatshirt, the T-shirt, the jeans he wore to Mass with the bulletin still folded in the back pocket — and there’s nothing to it. It’s a bath.
When he steps in and sits down behind her, the water climbs to within a finger of the rim and stops there, trembling, and the two of them hold very still and watch it.
“Archimedes,” she says, not moving.
“He ran down the street after. Naked. Yelling.”
“Del Playa’s seen worse. Don’t tempt me.”

The water is hot enough to sting. The porcelain where it rises out of the water behind him is cold as a church step, and she settles back against his chest between his knees with a long, contented noise, her pinned-up hair against his cheek and the knobs of her spine against his breastbone one at a time. He grew up in a house with one bathroom and two sisters, and nobody in it ever ran him a bath.

“Me first,” she says. She takes his right hand out of the water and puts it on her breast, and takes his left and puts it under the water between her thighs, and holds both of them there under her own. “Like that. Slow. Slower than that — like you’ve got all night. You’ve got all night.”

He does what she tells him. She’s specific about it, low against his jaw — *there*, and *lighter*, and *don’t get clever, just that, keep doing just that* — and after a little she takes her own hands away and leaves it to him. By now he has the rest of it by heart: where her breath catches and what it does when it catches, the way her heel comes up out of the water to hunt for the rim, the moment to change nothing at all. Her weight is all on him, slippery and warm, and every time she breathes he feels it the length of his own chest. The water rocks with her. It laps up the sides and over, and the candle on the floor leans and gutters in the wash, and she pushes back hard against him and comes with her head thrown back on his shoulder and her mouth open at his ear, and a wave of bathwater goes over the rim and across the tile.
She laughs after, breathless, against his jaw, while the water settles. “Look at you,” she says. “You used to be terrible at this.”
She turns her head on his shoulder until her mouth is at his ear. “Your turn. Out loud.”

choices.text: *Tell her exactly what you want. The whole sentence.*
response: So he tells her, start to finish, with his eyes on hers in the candlelight and nothing mumbled to the ceiling: he wants her mouth on him. Here, in the water. Slowly. And he wants to watch her do it.
Skye lifts her head off his shoulder to look at him. “Again,” she says. “The part about watching.”

He says it again. She listens to it like music she paid for. She turns in the water, slopping half the bath onto the floor, and kneels up between his knees with the candlelight on her wet shoulders, and takes him in her hand, and then in her mouth, slowly, her eyes on his face and not leaving it. The rim of the tub is under both his hands before he knows he’s reached for it. The harpsichord goes on picking its way down. She takes the time he asked for and more, until his head is back against the porcelain and her name is coming out of him in pieces — and then, on purpose, short of the end, she stops, and comes up, and wipes her mouth with the back of her wrist.
“Not in here,” she says. “I want the bed for that.”

She stands up out of the bath, and that’s when they find out the water has gone cold. She shivers from her knees to her shoulders and says something about it that would get her fired off *Sweetwater*.

choices.text: *Ask her to stand up and let you look at her.*
response: “Stand up,” he says. “Let me look at you.”

She stands up in the tub with the water running off her. In the candlelight she sets her hands on her hips and her chin up, a pinup off a calendar in a garage, and waits. He looks as long as he wants, and he tells her what he sees. Not the calendar. The water running down the middle of her and pooling in her navel. The gooseflesh coming up along her arms in the air off the window, and her nipples drawn tight with it. The pink line the rim of the tub left across the small of her back. The pencil in her hair, gone crooked, about to fall. A freckle on her hip he has never seen before and would like to stake a claim to. Somewhere around the freckle her hands come down off her hips and hang at her sides, and she quits posing and just stands there in the draft from the window and lets him.

He sits up in the water and puts his mouth on her where she stands, his hands on the backs of her thighs to keep her there. She gets one hand in his wet hair. The other goes out and finds the wall, the tile above the soap dish, and braces there, and her knees start to go, and he doesn’t let them; he holds her up and keeps on until she comes with her cheek almost to the tile and his name coming back off it.
When he sinks down again the water closes over him cold — it’s been cold for some time — and she’s shaking, and not all of it is that.

choices.text: *Ask for the thing you’ve been thinking about since Monday.*
response: “Monday,” he says. “Your mattress. You on top of me with my wrists in your hand, not letting me move.” He keeps his eyes on hers for the rest. “I’ve thought about it every day since. In the Commons. At the Anchor, holding a pie.”

She laughs, low, from the back of her throat. She turns over in the water to face him, takes his wrists, lays them along the rim of the tub on either side, and holds them there against the cold porcelain. She settles onto his lap — slick, weightless, everywhere at once, her breasts against his chest and her mouth at his ear telling him not to move — and moves against him in the water, slow and then not slow, and the bath goes over the rim in a wave and drowns the candle on the floor with a hiss. He pulls at her grip without meaning to. She tightens it and doesn’t stop —
— and stops. Lets go of his wrists. Sits back on her heels in water he only now notices has gone as cold as the Channel.
“Bed,” she says. “Now. You’re turning blue.”

s18.slug: SUNDAY · 10:30 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE NO
body: Her bed is the mattress on the floor under the open window, and the moon comes in over the sill and off the white wall onto the sheet, enough to see by and no more.

body.text: She finishes what she started in the tub. She’s unhurried about it now, kneeling over him in the light off the wall with her hair coming down out of the pencil around her face, no water to fight and nothing to brace against, and she makes it last. When he comes it’s with her name in his mouth — both of her names, *Skye* and then the other one, the one from the taquería, which he has never said in a bed before, and she hears it, and puts her face down on his stomach and laughs, shaking.

It’s her turn to look. She puts him on his back in the light off the wall and kneels beside him and takes as long as he did — longer — and doesn’t tell him one thing she sees, and he finds out from the other side what that costs. Then her mouth on him, unhurried, with her hand spread low on his stomach to keep him down on the sheet, until he comes under it, her name breaking in the middle on the way out of him.

She puts him on his back and pins his wrists to the mattress over his head the way he asked, one hand for both, and works her way down him with her mouth — his throat, his chest, his stomach — and when her reach runs out she brings his wrists down with her and holds them against his sides instead, and doesn’t let go of them until he’s come.

body: After that there’s no order to it and no hurry, and nobody’s turn. They trade. She says what she wants and he gives it to her, and he says what he wants and she gives it back, and some of it neither of them bothers to say. She lies on her side facing him and asks him to tell her what he’s going to do before he does it, every time, so she can wait for it — and he does, low, a sentence ahead of his hands all down the length of her, and she laughs at how good he’s got at it and then quits laughing. He asks for her hand on him while he watches her face, and gets it, slow, her eyes on his. He goes down on her in the moonlight with her knees up and her fingers in his hair, and this time she hardly directs him at all; she only says his name now and then, the way you’d say it into a dark house to check somebody’s home. When she comes it’s slow and long and nearly quiet, rolling up through her, her heel on his shoulder and her stomach trembling under his hand. Somewhere in there he finds the pencil, under his back, and she takes it out of his hand and throws it at the window.

Later — he couldn’t say how much later; the moon has gone some way along the wall — she’s over him. Her knees on either side of his hips. Her hands on his chest. Her hair all the way down now. Nothing on either of them, anywhere. She lowers herself along him until she’s lying on him from hip to breast, and there’s no air left between their bodies but in one place, and he can feel that one place exactly: the wet heat of her right there, a breath away from where all of him is straining up toward it, so near it’s hardly a distance at all. They’ve never been this close. He can see in her face that she knows it too. His hands are on her hips, his fingers spread over the bones of them, and they’re what’s holding it — his own two hands, keeping the last inch where it is while every other part of him argues with them. His forearms are shaking. Her breasts are against his chest and her heartbeat is going into him through them, fast, and the moon is on her back and her shoulders and in her loosened hair, and he can feel how little it would take — not a decision, hardly a motion, just his hands opening.
She’s breathing hard. She puts her mouth beside his ear.
“I want to have sex with you,” she says. “Now. Not tonight. Now.”
She says it into his ear with her eyes shut, and waits.

He doesn’t say anything. The surf comes up through the window and goes out again. A car goes by on Del Playa with its windows down and takes its radio with it. Her breath is on his neck, fast and then slower, waiting. Under his hands the long muscles of her hips tremble with holding still, and his hands don’t move.
In the silence he sees the aisle this morning: the walk back from the altar with the taste still in his mouth, and her in the pew ahead of him on her knees, not looking at him, looking at the altar.
“It’s still no,” he says. “For now.”
She goes on breathing against his neck. He can hear how that sounds, and she would hear him if he sanded it, so he says the rest.
“But it’s closer than it’s ever been.”

She lifts her head to look at him, her face just over his in the moonlight off the wall, close enough that he can see her eyes go from one of his to the other. He has one reason left, and she’s owed that too.
“I went up this morning.”

choices.key: Sunday night Skye asked, first, before anything. You told her it’s still no, for now — but closer than it’s ever been — and that the only thing holding it is that you went up this morning.
response: “I went up this morning,” he says again. “That’s all that’s holding it. That’s all there is.”
He doesn’t make it sound like more than it is. She’d hear that too. It’s this morning, and the Host, and the walk back down the aisle, and it’s the only thing in the room on his side.
She goes very still on him. Her hands come up off his chest and stay in the air above him, open, touching nothing.

choices.text: *Tell her what you want, all of it. Then the no.*
choices.key: Sunday night Skye asked, first, before anything. You told her everything you want — and then that it’s still no, for now, but closer than it’s ever been.
response: So he tells her what he wants, every piece of it, the man from the tub who can say things now. Her. The thing itself, tonight, with nothing in the way. To wake up here. To quit counting days. That he sat in the pew this morning with her beside him and wanted her between the readings, and went up anyway, and wanted her on the way back down the aisle. He doesn’t round any of it off. Then the no again, in the same voice, and why.
She puts her forehead down on his collarbone and keeps it there, and he feels her breathe out against his chest, long, down to the bottom of her.

choices.text: *Say it into her mouth. Don’t let go of her.*
choices.key: Sunday night Skye asked, first, before anything. You said no into her mouth — for now, closer than it’s ever been — and didn’t let go of her.
response: He pulls her mouth down to his and says it again into it, the no and the rest, with his hands still on her hips and holding: not letting her go, and not letting her one hair nearer. She kisses him through every word of it, hard, and her hips test his hands and find them right where they were.
She bites his lip, not gently, and keeps her teeth there while she breathes, and he can taste the bath on her. He bites her back.

s18a.slug: SUNDAY · 10:50 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — TO THE LETTER

body.text: “This morning,” she says. “That’s what’s holding it.” She counts something on his chest with one finger, and he knows it’s the days to next Sunday.
“You said all that,” she says into his collarbone, “and then you said no.” She lifts her head. She’s smiling.
“You bit me back,” she says. “That’s new.” She touches her lip.

body: “That wasn’t a no,” she says. “That was a *not tonight* holding its car keys.”
She tries his line in her own mouth, slowly, to hear what it sounds like there. “*Closer than it’s ever been.*” And she laughs, very low, and doesn’t get off him.
“Love is patient,” she says. “A man in a sport coat read it at me this morning. So now it’s official.”
“He read it at everybody.”
“He was looking at me.”
“Everybody looks at you.”
“Not like that. Like he was reading me my lines.” She leans down until her nose is against his and her eyes are too close to focus on. “I liked them,” she says. “I’m keeping them.”

She keeps the letter. She stays where she is, astride him, and his hands stay where they are, and the distance he named stays exactly what it was — and inside it she starts to move. Against him, never onto him: slow at first, the long slide of her along him and back, wet and hot and maddeningly patient, her palms spread on his chest and her eyes open on his, finding out how much there is to do in the room he’s left her. There’s a great deal. He finds that out too. She rocks and he rises to meet her and his hands hold and hold, his wrists aching with it and his fingers sunk in the give of her hips, and she laughs under her breath at how good it is, and then she isn’t laughing, and then it isn’t slow. The sheet is gone somewhere off the end of the mattress. The moon is on her shoulders and in the damp at her temples, and then she bends to him and her hair falls around both their faces and closes them in, and in the dark of it they breathe each other’s breath, mouths open and not kissing, until she comes with a sound into his mouth and he goes with her, right there against her, the two of them shaking together, his hands still on her hips and still holding.

Afterward they come apart. She slides off him onto her side and lies with her knee over his and her heart still going against his arm. While they weren’t looking the moon has come down off the wall, and it lies on the floorboards now among their clothes.

s18b.slug: SUNDAY · 11:45 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE QUESTION
body: It’s as dark in the room as it gets with the window open on Del Playa: the moon on the floor, a streetlight down at the corner, the white of the sheet. The lamp is off. The candles in the bathroom have burned down or drowned; he can’t smell them anymore. She’s lying on his chest with her ear over his heart, drawing something on his ribs with one fingernail, which he’s decided is the state of Ohio and which turns out, when he asks, to be a horse.
“Your mom went to see Danny today,” she says. “You said. What did he say?”
“Gina told him your name. Across the table. She told him about the picture.” He feels her go still to listen. “He said, *a NUN?*”

Skye laughs so hard she has to roll off him and put her face in the pillow to keep it off the street. He tells her the rest while she’s in there — that Danny laughed until the CO came over, that he wants to know what she lost the bet for — and every piece of it sends her back in.
She comes up out of the pillow wiping her eyes with the heel of her hand. “What *did* I lose the bet for?”
“He wants to know.”
“Tell him I’m still deciding.” She settles back down on him, her cheek on his chest again. “I like your brother.”
“He thinks I must’ve tricked you somehow.”
“Into what?”
“Any of it.”
She thinks that over with her chin on his breastbone. “Tell him it was the flannel,” she says.

She’s quiet after that, her ear back over his heart, long enough that he thinks she’s gone to sleep. “It’s slow now,” she says at last, about the heart. “It was very fast before. I was keeping track.” The fingernail goes back to the horse. The surf comes up through the window, and a gust off the water lifts the curtain and lets it down.
“What was the question?” she says. “The one I’m the answer to.”
She doesn’t lift her head. The fingernail has stopped on his ribs, wherever the horse’s heart would be.
He gives her Nonna’s.
“She asked me what makes me pray.”
The fingernail doesn’t move.
“Do I?”
“Yes.”

It’s true. He prays for her at red lights, in the space between the red and the green. He has prayed for her by name. And this morning on his knees beside her, with the Host still on his tongue, he said her name again — both of them, now.
“What do you say?” she says. “When you do it. For me.”
“A Hail Mary. Your name. Then whatever I want for you that day.”
“Like what?”
“That you sleep. That your mother calls less.” He thinks about it. “That Corinne gets a cold.”
Her head comes up. “You pray for Corinne to get a cold.”
“A small one. Over a weekend.”
She puts her head back down, and he feels her smile against his chest, and then he feels it go.
“You’re going Wednesday,” she says.
“Yes.”
“And you have to tell him you won’t do it again. That’s the rule. The purpose part.” She waits until he says yes to that too. “And then you come back here.”
“Yes.”

“I’m not mad at it.” She says it fast. “I want you to know that. I came to your Mass. I knelt. I’d do it again next Sunday, I’d do it every Sunday, I liked it, I liked watching you go up. That isn’t the part.”
She comes up on one elbow, and he can see the shine of her eyes in the dark and not much else.
“So here’s mine,” she says. “When it’s yes —”
*When*, she says, and he doesn’t correct her.

“— am I only ever going to be something you carry into that little room on a Wednesday?” Her voice doesn’t go up at the end. “You go in and say me to a man behind a screen, and he tells you what I cost, and you come out, and you get to go up on Sunday. And I’m still here. I’m always still here.”

body.text: “I can live in the daylight column,” she says. “I told you I could. But this isn’t daylight, Jack. I’ll be in the bad column on a Wednesday every week of my life with you.”
body.else: “I’ll be the thing you tell him about on a Wednesday,” she says. “Every week of my life with you.”

body: She’s quiet. Her heart is going against his ribs, fast for somebody lying still.

“Monday I didn’t finish something,” she says. “I said I didn’t want to be the occasion. I had the rest of it right there, and I put it back, because it wasn’t ready.” She takes a breath. “It’s ready.”
“I want to be the good thing,” she says. “With the lights off.”
The lights are off.

There’s one answer in him. It has a priest in it, and a vow, and a church she knelt in this morning for his sake and doesn’t believe a word of. He can’t put that in her hands at midnight in the dark with nothing on and call it an answer. She’s waiting. He can hear the surf, and her breathing, and his own heart under her ear, and none of it is going to say anything for him.

choices.text: “You’re the good thing. You’re the good thing *now*.”
choices.key: In the dark Skye asked what question she’s the answer to, and said she wants to be the good thing with the lights off. You told her she’s the good thing now.
response: She doesn’t answer. Her hand comes looking for his in the dark, and finds it, and brings it down and holds it on her stomach, under her own, the way she held his hands in the bath, only now there is nothing she wants him to do with it. Her thumb goes back and forth over his knuckles, slowly, like she’s counting them to be sure they’re all there.

choices.text: “I don’t know how to make you not that. I’m trying to find out.”
choices.key: In the dark Skye asked what question she’s the answer to, and said she wants to be the good thing with the lights off. You told her you don’t know how yet — you’re trying to find out.
response: “Okay,” she says. “Find out fast.”
She puts her head back down on his chest. After a moment, smaller, into his skin: “I mean it about fast.”
And later, when he thinks she’s asleep: “Anybody else I know would’ve had an answer. A good one. I’d have believed it for a week.”

choices.text: “Then we’ll have to keep the lights off.”
choices.key: In the dark Skye asked what question she’s the answer to, and said she wants to be the good thing with the lights off. You made a joke about the lights. She laughed, and then she didn’t.
response: She laughs, and then she doesn’t, and then she turns over with her back against his chest and pulls his arm over her and holds it there by the wrist.
“That was a good one,” she says, with her back to him. “I’m going to need a better one.”

s19.slug: MONDAY · 12:50 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM
body: She falls asleep first. He feels it happen, her breathing going long against him and her hand going heavy where it lies, and just before she’s gone she says one more thing.

body.text: “Now,” she says, to nobody, already mostly gone.
“Lights,” she says, already mostly gone, and doesn’t finish it.

body: Her hair against his mouth smells of the bath and the candles. The moon is going west off the floor, leaving the boards to the dark a little at a time. His jeans are where he dropped them by the mattress, with the RAZR in the pocket. Downstairs Tomás’s stereo has been off for an hour, and the house is down to its own noises: the old refrigerator in the kitchen, the wind trying Sol’s swing on its chains out on the porch. Delgado is a long cold walk up Ocean Road, and she is warm all down his side, and her mouth has come a little open against his shoulder, and in the moonlight off the floor he can see the crease the pillow is starting on her cheek.

choices.key: Sunday night you stayed. Just sleep.
Sunday night you went home, like last time.

s19s.slug: MONDAY · 1:10 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM
body: He stays.

He lies on his back in her bed with nothing on either of them and her asleep against him, and sleep is all it is; he keeps it to that. Her knee is over his. Her hand is open on his chest where it fell, and now and then the fingers move a little, still drawing horses. The moon has gone off the floor, and the window is full of it instead, and the curtain lifts in the air off the water and settles again. He isn’t tired at all.
He says a Hail Mary for her under his breath, the red-light kind, fast, with her name on the end of it. And another one, slower, that isn’t for her.
She stirs. She doesn’t open her eyes. Into his shoulder, half asleep, she says, “Mary Catherine says goodnight.”
“Goodnight,” he tells her. Both of them.
She smiles without waking, or he thinks she does; in the dark he can’t be sure of anything but the weight of her, and the warmth, and her breath going slow against his collarbone.

On the floor by the mattress his jeans buzz against the boards. He reaches down one-armed without waking her, fishes the RAZR out of the pocket, and opens it low against his chest so the screen won’t find her face. One from before midnight he never heard, and two just now.

body.text: she woke me up for this
nonna says maria caterina is a good name for a wife

body: It’s after four on Glenwood. The furnace won’t have kicked on yet, and Nonna is up in the dark at the kitchen table with her beads.

He leaves Theo’s where it is. He closes the phone and puts it back in the jeans and lies down again, and Skye turns her face into his shoulder in her sleep. Her hand on his chest closes a little, around nothing, the way a sleeping kid’s hand closes on a finger.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. s19h.slug: MONDAY · 1:15 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE → OCEAN ROAD
body: She walks him down. She goes ahead of him on the stairs in his flannel and nothing else, buttoned wrong, past Tomás’s dark door and across the front room and out onto the porch, and at the top step she stops with one hand on the post. Sol’s swing is moving a little on its new chains in the wind off the water.

body.text: “Like last time,” she says, and pulls the flannel together at her throat. “I liked last time. Go before I quit liking it.”
body.else: “Go home, Youngstown,” she says, and pulls the flannel together at her throat. “Before I change my mind about letting you.”

body: He goes down the steps. When he looks back from the street she’s still up there, a white shirt in the dark of the porch, watching him go.

He goes up Del Playa with his hands in the pocket of his sweatshirt — a couch on somebody’s lawn, a porch light left burning, a cooler tipped over in the gutter, the surf under the bluff louder than it ever is by day — and turns onto Ocean Road. St. Brendan’s is dark on the hill, the bell tower black against a sky the moon has washed almost white, the doors shut on the place where he knelt this morning. He knows it’s there without looking. The urge to turn around is in his legs the whole way up Ocean Road, in the backs of his knees and the soles of his feet, every step of it one his legs take against their will.
Under a streetlight on Ocean Road he opens the RAZR. Three he never heard: one from before midnight, two from after one.

body.text: she woke me up for this
nonna says maria caterina is a good name for a wife

body: Nonna is up with her beads before the furnace, then. It’s after four on Glenwood.
Room 412 is dark, and Theo is awake in it. He’s on his back in his bed with the blanket to his chin, and in the light from the hall Jack can see that his eyes are open.
“Home,” Jack says.
Theo says nothing at all. His eyes stay on Jack in the dark while Jack gets his shoes off, and while he gets into bed, and after.
